name: Aleksander Petrov
habitus: Working out, Playing chess, Playing video games

Black: They had black hair, the kind that looks planned even in a hurry.
Black hair, neat enough to make the rest of the room feel underdressed.
I remember black hair and the attitude of someone who trusts shadows more than sunlight.
Brown: Brown hair, the forgettable kind—if the rest of them weren’t so suspicious.
Their brown hair was boring. Their timing was not.
I’d call the hair ‘brown’ and the behavior ‘questionable’.
Blonde: Blonde hair, the shade people dye for. This one wore it like a warning sign.
They had blonde hair and the confidence of someone who’s never lost in a crowd.
Hard to miss: blonde hair, sharp eyes, and no patience for small talk.
Red: Red hair, the kind you remember even if you’re trying not to remember anything.
They had red hair and the expression of someone who starts fires metaphorically—and maybe literally.
Bright red hair, like they didn’t understand the concept of ‘low profile’.

Blue: Blue eyes that scanned the room like it was a crime scene waiting for a crime.
Their blue eyes were calm. Too calm for someone in that much of a hurry.
I remember blue eyes that smiled a lot less than their mouth did.
Brown: Brown eyes, steady and unreadable, like they’d practiced in a mirror.
They had brown eyes and the habit of looking at exits more than people.
Those brown eyes measured everything—doors, cameras, and me included.
Green: Green eyes, the curious kind, always counting, weighing, judging.
Their green eyes flicked over details like they were taking mental notes.
I remember green eyes that looked amused, even when nothing was funny.
Hazel: Hazel eyes, always shifting, like they hadn’t decided who to lie to yet.
They had hazel eyes and the reflex of checking reflections in every window.
Hazel eyes that softened when they smiled and hardened when money came up.

Big forehead: Hard to miss that big forehead, like their brain needed a penthouse.
They had a big forehead and the habit of frowning like the world owed them answers.
Big forehead, bigger attitude. The combination tends to cause trouble.
Tattoo: They had a visible tattoo they clearly wanted people to notice and remember.
I spotted a tattoo peeking from under the sleeve—subtle is not their brand.
One tattoo, carefully placed, like a signature they forgot to hide.
Rainbow hair streak: There was a rainbow streak in their hair, as if subtlety had been fired years ago.
A rainbow streak in the hair tends to stand out, even in a crowd of suspects.
They had this rainbow hair streak that screamed ‘look at me’ while they pretended not to.
Necklace: They kept touching a necklace, like it was either sentimental or stolen.
I remember a necklace that looked too expensive for their story.
They had a habit of fiddling with a necklace while lying. Very convenient for me.
Scar: They had a scar that said ‘long story’ and a face that said ‘don’t ask’.
A thin scar, neatly healed, the kind you don’t get from clumsiness.
Their scar caught the light every time they turned their head away from the truth.
Moustache: They had a moustache, carefully groomed, like it had its own agenda.
I remember the moustache. It entered the room a second before the rest of them.
That moustache looked trustworthy. They did not.
Beard: They wore a beard that tried very hard to look respectable.
A neat beard, trimmed to suggest order. The rest of them disagreed.
Their beard covered half their face, but not the guilt.
Glasses: Glasses, stylish and just reflective enough to hide where their eyes really went.
They adjusted their glasses every time the questions got too precise.
Those glasses said ‘researcher’. Their pacing said ‘runner’.
Earrings: I noticed a pair of earrings that looked too expensive for their plane ticket.
They had earrings that jingled louder than their conscience.
Earrings that caught the light every time they looked for exits.
Goatee: They sported a goatee, the universal symbol for ‘trust me, I’ve made choices’.
I remember the goatee. It tried to make them look intellectual.
Their goatee was perfectly shaped. Their story wasn’t.
Long hair: They had long hair tied back just enough to look practical, not enough to look innocent.
Long hair, always pushed behind the ear when they lied.
Their long hair moved a lot. Their answers, not so much.

Canadian: Their accent was Canadian, polite even when their story wasn’t.
They apologized twice while lying. Classic Canadian accent, less classic honesty.
You could hear the Canadian in their vowels and the trouble in their timing.
Mexican: They spoke with a Mexican accent and the rhythm of someone used to bargaining.
That warm Mexican accent almost distracted from the sharpness of their answers.
Their Mexican accent wrapped around every word like it was negotiating with me.
Australian: They had an Australian accent and the relaxed tone of someone who shouldn’t be that relaxed.
That Australian accent made every joke sound friendlier than it should have.
Their Australian accent dropped consonants and, occasionally, truths.
American: They spoke with an American accent, fast and confident, like the world was an argument they planned to win.
That American accent came with big gestures and bigger claims.
Their American accent filled the room. Their answers tried to fill the gaps.
Dutch: They had a Dutch accent and the calm of someone who has already checked every exit.
That Dutch accent carried a certain bluntness I almost respected.
Their Dutch accent made their questions sound practical. Their motives, less so.
British: They spoke with a British accent sharp enough to cut through my patience.
That British accent made every insult sound like a compliment with bad timing.
Their British accent tried to sound charming. Their alibi did not.
German: They had a German accent and answered like they were ticking boxes on an invisible form.
That German accent clipped every word neatly, like they hated wasting syllables.
Their German accent made even small talk sound like a briefing.
Polish: They spoke with a Polish accent and the kind of dry humour you only get from long winters.
That Polish accent came with precise words and carefully imprecise answers.
Their Polish accent softened only when they mentioned home. Everything else stayed sharp.
Russian: They had a Russian accent and a habit of pausing before every important word.
That Russian accent wrapped around the truth like it was smuggling it.
Their Russian accent made every sentence sound like it had a backup plan.
Italian: They spoke with an Italian accent and gestured like they were conducting an invisible orchestra.
That Italian accent turned every denial into a small performance.
Their Italian accent made ‘no comment’ sound almost charming.
Irish: They had an Irish accent and a talent for turning answers into stories.
That Irish accent danced around the question more than it answered it.
Their Irish accent made excuses sound like folk tales.
Belarussian: They spoke with a Belarussian accent and the calm of someone used to cold weather and warm problems.
That Belarussian accent kept their voice low, but their eyes did most of the talking.
Their Belarussian accent carried a kind of quiet stubbornness I’ve seen in reports, not tourists.
French: They had a French accent and a talent for making complaints sound poetic.
That French accent rolled over the words, especially the ones they wanted me to ignore.
Their French accent made even lies sound like they came with a wine pairing.

Lockpicking: Their hands moved like someone who’s very familiar with locks and the concept of ‘private’.
They talked about doors the way poets talk about sunsets. I got suspicious.
I noticed how they glanced at every lock in the room like it was a challenge.
Disguise: They had the posture of someone who’s worn a lot of faces to work.
Their outfit was forgettable in a way that takes serious practice.
They kept adjusting their collar like they weren’t entirely used to this version of themselves.
Stealth: They moved so quietly I almost forgot they were there. My notebook didn’t.
Their footsteps were softer than their lies.
You don’t learn to move that silently by accident.
Languages: They switched languages mid-sentence just to check if I was paying attention.
Their suitcase contained more phrasebooks than shirts.
People who speak that many languages rarely run out of excuses.
Negotiation: They tried to negotiate with me like this was a marketplace, not an interview.
Every answer came with a counter-offer.
They smiled in the way only professional negotiators and salespeople do.
Intimidation: They leaned in just a little too close, like they thought fear was a shortcut.
Their silence was loud, the kind people use instead of threats.
They stared like they were used to winning staring contests and arguments.
Hacking: They talked about computers the way some people talk about pets they slightly fear.
Their fingers twitched like they missed a keyboard.
Anyone who smiles while saying ‘I could fix that from here’ is either a hacker or a liar. Sometimes both.
Electronics: They noticed every camera in the room before they noticed me.
Their eyes kept drifting to the wiring like they were mentally redrawing it.
They called the alarm system ‘cute’. I made a note of that.
Surveillance: They chose the seat with the best view of every door without thinking about it.
Their eyes kept tracking reflections in glass and metal surfaces.
They have the stillness of someone used to watching, not being watched.
Investigation: They asked more questions than I did, which is never a good sign.
Their notes were more detailed than some of my colleagues’ reports.
They spotted inconsistencies in the story before I finished telling it.
Interrogation: They treated conversation like a chess match: always planning three questions ahead.
They let silences hang just a bit too long, like they were waiting for me to fill them.
They looked more comfortable on my side of the table than I did.
Deduction: They kept finishing my sentences. I don’t like competition.
Their eyes lit up every time a detail didn’t fit. They live for that.
They connected dots I hadn’t even put on the board yet.
Forgery: They admired the signatures on the wall a little too closely.
Their compliments about our document security felt… professional.
They handled paper like it was both a weapon and a weakness.
Art history: They kept correcting the dates under paintings nobody else noticed.
Their eyes lingered on frames and brushstrokes more than people.
They called one forgery ‘insulting’. I wrote that down.
Research: They arrived overprepared, the curse of professional researchers.
Their folder of notes had footnotes. Footnotes, detective.
They cited sources while giving an alibi.
Martial arts: They moved like someone counting exits and angles, not chairs.
Their stance shifted every time someone entered the room.
You don’t get muscles like that from typing.
Survival skills: They looked at the room like they were ranking it for shelter potential.
They asked where the nearest water source was. Indoors.
Their clothes were more practical than fashionable. Never a coincidence.
Tracking: They noticed footprints on the floor no one else cared about.
Their questions were all about routes, not reasons.
They traced imaginary paths in the air while talking.
Parkour: They sized up walls and balconies like they were reviewing a menu.
Their shoes looked ready for running, climbing, or both.
They mentioned ‘shortcuts’ in a way that made me check the rooftops.
Acrobatics: They moved their weight from foot to foot with circus-level balance.
Chairs, railings, and ledges all got a quick professional once-over.
Their idea of ‘stretching’ looked suspiciously like a warm-up routine.
Firearms: They checked every ‘no weapons’ sign like it was a personal challenge.
Their fingers did that invisible trigger squeeze when they were thinking.
They asked too many questions about the security distance to the exits.
Tactical planning: They rearranged sugar packets on the table into formations. I noticed.
Their questions were all about timing, routes, and who knew what when.
They seemed more interested in the layout than the conversation.

Smoking: They smelled faintly of smoke and bad decisions.
Their fingers had that telltale stain you don’t get from coffee.
They kept reaching for a cigarette that wasn’t there. Nervous habit.
Drinking: They talked about bars more than museums.
Their breath carried the memory of something stronger than coffee.
They knew more about local drinks than local laws.
Gambling: They shuffled coasters like cards and eyed everyone’s watches.
They described risk the way most people describe hobbies.
They kept asking about odds in a conversation that wasn’t a game.
Tattoos: They had ink peeking out from under their sleeves, like secrets that ran out of space.
Their tattoos looked carefully chosen, not spontaneous.
They traced old lines on their skin when the questions got close.
Piercings: They had more metal than most jewellery displays.
Their piercings caught the light every time they dodged a question.
You could hear a faint jingle when they lied.
Reading: They carried a book everywhere, like a shield.
Their answers came with references nobody asked for.
They looked more at the printed page than at people.
Gaming: They compared this interview to a boss fight. Charming.
Their reflexes said ‘gamer’. Their sense of reality… less so.
They talked about strategies like this was just another level.
Coding: They spoke about bugs and features the way some people talk about sins and excuses.
Their hands twitched like they were typing ghost code.
They described their alibi like a changelog.
Watching movies: They kept comparing everything to films. Including their own life choices.
Half their references were movie quotes. The other half were spoilers.
They said this whole thing ‘felt like a crime thriller’. I agreed.
Yoga: They sat too straight for someone allegedly relaxed.
Their breathing stayed suspiciously calm under pressure.
They mentioned chakras while I mentioned handcuffs.
Meditation: They paused before every answer like they were checking in with their inner lawyer.
Their calm felt practiced, like a habit, not a personality.
They suggested I ‘breathe through the tension’. I suggested they answer the question.
Cooking: They described meals in more detail than their alibi.
Their hands smelled faintly of spices and suspicion.
They said stress made them want to cook. I said it made me want to arrest people.
Joking: They used jokes as a shield, which works better at parties than in interviews.
Every serious question got a punchline before an answer.
Their humour was good. Their timing, less so.
Pranks: They treated everything like a setup for a prank. Including this.
They smirked like they were waiting for someone to say ‘gotcha’.
Their idea of ‘just a joke’ usually leaves paperwork.
Flirting: They tried to flirt their way through the questions. Classic, ineffective.
Compliments instead of answers—that’s a style, not a defence.
They treated eye contact like a weapon and a hobby.
Hiking: Their boots looked more ready for trails than city streets.
They complained the room had ‘no fresh air, no views, no point’.
They measured distance in ‘short walks’ I wouldn’t attempt without training.
Camping: They smelled faintly of smoke and pine, like they’d slept closer to trees than walls.
They asked where the nearest campsite was. Indoors.
They rated the chairs for ‘sleep potential’ out of habit.
Fishing: They compared patience in this interview to waiting for a bite.
Their stories involved more lakes than witnesses.
They said they preferred quiet places. I said I preferred clear answers.
Skateboarding: They bounced on their heels like any moment could turn into a ramp.
Their shoes had more scuffs than most crime scenes.
They described routes in terms of ‘good spots’ and ‘bad landings’.
Dancing: They moved even when standing still, like there was always music somewhere.
They turned dodging questions into a choreography.
They marked time with their foot, not the clock.
Street art: Their hands were stained with colours that don’t come off easily.
They kept glancing at blank walls like they were unfinished business.
They called one alley ‘a missed canvas’. I called it ‘evidence’.
Shooting: They talked about firing ranges the way some people talk about spa days.
They handled imaginary weight in their hands, like muscle memory.
They knew more about calibres than I strictly needed.
Traveling: They listed countries faster than I could list charges.
Their passport was heavier than their conscience.
They called this ‘just another stop’. I called it ‘a problem’.
Exploring: They described cities like puzzles they hadn’t finished yet.
They get lost on purpose. People like that find trouble accidentally.
They called alleys ‘invitations’. I called them ‘crime scenes waiting’.
Watching Movies: They claimed to ‘study’ people through films. I reminded them this wasn’t a rehearsal.
They compared my questions to plot twists. I took that as a compliment.
Every reference was a movie. Every excuse, a rerun.
Eating out: They remembered restaurants better than dates.
Their alibi involved more menus than witnesses.
They rated the neighbourhood in food, not safety.
Working out: They rolled their shoulders like they missed a gym more than their conscience.
Their knuckles looked like they’d met a few bad ideas up close.
They asked about the nearest gym before a lawyer.
Playing chess: They treated every question like a move two turns ahead.
They stared at the table like there were invisible pieces on it.
They talked about sacrifices with alarming enthusiasm.
Playing video games: They kept calling this ‘a side quest’. I strongly disagreed.
Their metaphors were all levels, bosses, and loot.
They asked if there was a ‘skip dialogue’ option. There is not.
Shopping: They could list brands faster than dates and times.
Their bags had more receipts than answers.
They called this ‘a bad customer experience’. I called it ‘an interrogation’.
Stealth: They moved like they were trying not to exist, which is rarely innocent.
They stood where shadows fell naturally.
They apologised when they made even the slightest sound.
Reading, Writing: They took notes during the questions. That’s usually my job.
They corrected my grammar once. I let them live—for now.
They said they ‘process things better in writing’. I gave them a statement form.
